title: In the LORD I Take Refuge

verses.text: In the LORD I take refuge. How then can you say to me: "Flee like a bird to your mountain!
For behold, the wicked bend their bows. They set their arrow on the string to shoot from the shadows at the upright in heart.
If the foundations are destroyed, what can the righteous do?"
The LORD is in His holy temple; the LORD is on His heavenly throne. His eyes are watching closely; they examine the sons of men.
The LORD tests the righteous and the wicked; His soul hates the lover of violence.
On the wicked He will rain down fiery coals and sulfur; a scorching wind will be their portion.
For the LORD is righteous; He loves justice. The upright will see His face.

context.author: The title says “of David” (Hebrew le-David), which can mean by David, for David or about David. Seventy-three psalms carry his name; tradition and the New Testament take many of them as his.
context.genre: Psalm: a song or prayer in Hebrew poetry
context.audience: Israel at worship in Jerusalem, and every reader who prays
context.setting: “In the LORD I take refuge. How then can you say to me: Flee like a bird to your mountain!” (v.1). Friends warn David that the wicked have strung their bows to shoot the upright from the shadows, and ask, “If the foundations are destroyed, what can the righteous do?” (v.3). David answers by looking up: “The LORD is in His holy temple; the LORD is on His heavenly throne” (v.4). His eyes examine everyone; He tests the righteous and the wicked (vv.4-5). Fire and sulfur will fall on the wicked (v.6), but “the upright will see His face” (v.7).
context.custom: Birds chased by hunters fled to the hills (1 Samuel 26:20, where David calls himself a partridge hunted on the mountains). Archers hid among rocks and shadows to ambush travelers. The “foundations” (v.3) are the pillars of society: law, justice and order. A cup or portion (v.6) was the share a host poured for each guest; here it is the share of judgment.
context.timelineImmediate: Psalm 12 cries for help when the faithful have vanished and every tongue flatters.
context.timelineBible: The fire and sulfur of v.6 recall the judgment on Sodom (Genesis 19:24). Habakkuk echoes v.4: “the LORD is in His holy temple; let all the earth be silent before Him” (Habakkuk 2:20). Jesus promised, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God” (Matthew 5:8), the hope of v.7.

translation.meaning: To flee for protection, to shelter in. David will not flee to the hills; he has a better refuge.
Palace, temple. God’s holy dwelling, here His heavenly palace.
To test, examine, prove, as metal is tried.

gospelParallels.note: The pure in heart will see God.
Sodom an example, and the Lord rescues the godly.

otBackground.note: The LORD is in His holy temple.
Hunting a partridge in the mountains.

overview.summary: Told to flee like a bird, David stays put: the LORD is on His throne, tests every heart, and the upright will see His face.

archaeology.t: Iron Age arrowheads, some inscribed with owners’ names, are known from Canaan and Lebanon.
Caves in the Judean hills sheltered people in times of danger.

overview.discussion: “If the foundations are destroyed, what can the righteous do?” (v.3). When things fall apart, where do I look first?
overview.book: The book of Psalms · 150 psalms (1-100 in the app so far). Israel’s songs and prayers: praise, lament, thanks, trust and wisdom, many of them by David.
overview.author: David

historicalImage.caption: King David Playing the Harp, by Gerard van Honthorst (1622, Centraal Museum, Utrecht). Seventy-three psalms carry David’s name in their titles, and 1 Samuel 16:23 remembers him as a skilled player of the lyre.

currentImage.caption: The view down from Masada above the Dead Sea, with the siege ramp the Romans built in AD 73-74. The name Masada comes from the Hebrew metsudah, “fortress,” the word David uses in Psalm 18:2: “The LORD is my rock, my fortress, and my deliverer.” David hid in the strongholds of this wilderness when Saul hunted him (1 Samuel 23:29).
